facts.text: Champlain, Virginia, may have taken its name from England’s Essex County or from the Duke of Essex when the county was split in 1692.
Matthew’s Church and the nearby Linden are both listed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving Champlain’s colonial heritage.
Champlain grew into a colonial trade hub, with Layton’s Landing Wharf and Ferry linking inland farms to ports like Tappahannock and Fredericksburg.
By the mid‑1700s, Layton’s Landing housed a tobacco warehouse, merchant stores, and an inn, later becoming a steamboat stop until 1937.
The community sits at the crossroads of U.S. Route 17, known as the Tidewater Trail, and Virginia State Route 631, a quiet rural junction.
Champlain experiences a humid subtropical climate, with July highs around 88°F and January lows near 28°F, and averages 43.5 inches of rain yearly.
